Case file — System Analysis & Design

How do you turn an online fresh-food store into a buildable spec?

Team project (3) · Sep–Nov 2024

SunFresh — Agricultural Products E-commerce Website

3 user roles · 11 modules · 19 use cases · 18 tables · supervised by a university lecturer

An online store for clean agricultural products, with one site for customers and another for admin and staff. We went from business analysis to a working Laravel application: requirements, use cases, process flows, the database, and features such as VNPay payment, promotions, stock and returns.

Use CaseActivity & SequenceERD / CDMMySQLLaravelBootstrapVNPay
My role
  1. Led the business analysis for both the customer site and the admin site, planned the project and split the tasks across the team.
  2. Analyzed the data and created the MySQL tables with primary keys, foreign keys and constraints, based on the team's ERD and CDM.
  3. Worked on the specification set: 11 use case diagrams, 19 use case specifications (priority, preconditions, main and alternative flows), 19 activity and 19 sequence diagrams.
  4. Defined business rules and validations: price in multiples of 1,000 VND, return window of 0–7 days, product image up to 2 MB, activation link valid for 60 minutes.
  5. Built product management, the customer product pages, checkout, product reviews, revenue and best-seller statistics, and promotion handling in the cart.
19 use cases: each with priority, preconditions, main and alternative flows.
Order lifecycle: pending, packing, shipping, delivered, plus return and refund.
3 roles: Admin, Staff and Customer with role-based permissions.
Problems and how I handled them
ProblemReturns have rules that pull against each other: only delivered orders qualify, the window is 0–7 days, and some products cannot be returned at all.
What I didI wrote them as explicit business rules in the use case and designed the return screen to list eligible, expired and non-returnable items separately, so a customer cannot pick something the rules reject.
ProblemAdmin, Staff and Customer share the same data, so loose permissions could expose it.
What I didI defined what each role can access and wrote it into the specification.
ProblemAn order moves through pending, packing, shipping and delivered, and returns and refunds depend on that status.
What I didI mapped the lifecycle as a business process, and each use case states the status it needs (for example, returns only for delivered orders).

Case file — Product Documentation

What does a returns feature look like as a PRD?

Sample document · drafted with AI, checked by me

PRD — Return & Refund Request (SunFresh)

Based on use case UC13 · Actors: Customer, Staff, Admin · Status: sample

I rewrote my own UC13 use case as a short PRD with user stories, acceptance criteria and a low-fidelity wireframe. Items marked proposed are my additions to the original specification, not part of the delivered system.

Problem and goal

Fresh-food customers need a clear way to report defective goods and get their money back. Without one, complaints go through chat or phone, evidence is lost, and staff cannot track which items were picked up and refunded. Goal: let a customer submit a return with evidence, and let admin and staff review, collect and refund it in one tracked flow.

User stories and acceptance criteria
User storyAcceptance criteria
US1 · Customer. As a customer with a delivered order, I want to select defective items and attach photos or video, so that I can get a refund.
  • Given an order with status "delivered successfully", when I open my order history, then a Return button appears on that order.
  • Items inside the 0–7 day return window are listed as selectable; expired and non-returnable items are listed separately and cannot be selected.
  • A reason and at least one selected item are required; images and video are optional.
  • On submit, the request is saved as pending and sent to staff.
US2 · Admin. As an admin, I want to review a return request and assign someone to collect the goods, so that returns are handled quickly.
  • Admin sees the reason, images, video and items of each pending request.
  • Admin confirms the request and assigns a staff member for pickup.
  • Admin can reject a request with a written reason, which the customer can see. proposed
US3 · Staff. As a staff member, I want to mark goods as collected and complete the refund, so that the customer is paid back.
  • Staff marks the request as "goods collected".
  • The return record is stored and the refund to the customer is recorded.
  • The customer can see the final status of the request.
Business rules
  • A return can only be created for orders in the "delivered successfully" status; unconfirmed orders can only be cancelled.
  • The return window is 0–7 days, and some products are marked as non-returnable.
  • The customer must be logged in; order and return data must be available.
Edge cases to resolve
  • Every item in the order is outside the window: disable the submit button and explain why. proposed
  • The same item is submitted twice: block a second request while one is pending. proposed
  • Refund method differs between VNPay and cash on delivery orders: to be confirmed with the business. open question
  • Upload limits for return images and video: to be decided. open question

  1. Reason is mandatory; media upload is optional but encouraged as evidence.
  2. Only items inside the window can be ticked, so the customer cannot request something the rules reject.
  3. Ineligible items stay visible and greyed out, so the customer understands why they are excluded.
  4. One submit action creates a pending request and notifies staff.
Problems and how I handled them
ProblemAn AI draft can include behaviour the real system does not have.
What I didI checked every point against my UC13 specification, kept what matched, and labelled my additions as proposed.
ProblemSome questions cannot be answered from the spec, such as the refund method for VNPay versus cash on delivery orders.
What I didI listed them as open questions to confirm with the business instead of guessing.
How I used AI
Tool: Claude. Method: I gave the model my original UC13 specification and the return screen, asked for draft user stories, acceptance criteria and edge cases, then checked every point against UC13. I kept what matched the real flow and labelled everything I added as proposed or as an open question.
Case file — Customer Churn Prediction

Which households are about to churn — and why?

Solo project · Aug–Sep 2025

Dunnhumby Customer Churn Prediction — SQL Server, Statistical Testing & Power BI

2,500 households · 2.6M transactions · 2-year retail panel (Dunnhumby "The Complete Journey")

A churn-prediction pipeline on real retail transaction data: a SQL Server ETL, leakage-safe feature engineering, statistical hypothesis tests and a tuned XGBoost model. It ends in a 4-page Power BI dashboard that shows which households to contact first.

SQL ServerSQLAlchemyPythonscikit-learnXGBoostChi-square / ANOVAPower BI
  1. Built a SQL Server ETL pipeline (extract, transform, load) with SQLAlchemy. I validated 2.6M transaction rows with SQL aggregation and flagged outliers with the IQR rule, then looked into the cause of each before deciding to keep or drop it.
  2. Defined churn as no purchases at all in the final 2 weeks of the observation window. Built 10 feature groups (campaign/coupon engagement, store affinity, category mix, discount sensitivity, spend-recency trend), all computed from data before the label cutoff to avoid leakage.
  3. Ran Chi-square and one-way ANOVA tests with Bonferroni correction across the candidate features and kept the statistically significant predictors, alongside features chosen on business judgment.
  4. Tuned an XGBoost classifier with GridSearchCV (RepeatedStratifiedKFold, average-precision scoring) and used the F1-optimal threshold instead of the default 0.5. Compared it with Logistic Regression and Random Forest to weigh the interpretability trade-offs.
  5. Built a 4-page Power BI dashboard: churn overview, recency analysis, campaign effectiveness, and a household worklist ranked by predicted churn probability.
19x higher risk: households fully inactive for 4 weeks vs. those active every week (77.7% vs 4.1% churn).
Recency = 56% of model importance — the single strongest churn predictor, ahead of total purchase history.
8x lower churn: households that received Campaign 25 churned at 4.8% vs. 37.1% for those who didn't.
Problems and how I handled them
ProblemIQR flags outliers, but an outlier can be a data error or a genuine purchase.
What I didI traced each case to its cause before deciding to keep or drop it, instead of removing them all.
ProblemChurn is defined by the last 2 weeks, so any feature that touches that period gives away the answer.
What I didEvery feature is computed only from data before the label cutoff.
ProblemThe default 0.5 cutoff is not tied to this problem.
What I didI tuned with average-precision scoring and chose the threshold that maximizes F1.
ProblemTesting many candidate features at once makes false positives likely.
What I didI applied Bonferroni correction to the Chi-square and ANOVA tests.

Case file — Retail Analytics

Where is the Superstore actually losing money?

Solo project · Jun–Jul 2025

Superstore Sales Analytics & Customer Segmentation

9,994 orders · 793 customers · US market, 2011–2014

Four years of retail transactions, cleaned and run through EDA, RFM customer segmentation and an interactive Power BI dashboard, to show where the store makes and loses money and which customers to target.

PythonpandasPower BIDAXRFM
  1. Cleaned data types, dropped redundant columns and checked Sales, Quantity and Profit for invalid values.
  2. Added Profit Margin and Discount Range features and broke profitability down by category, region and segment.
  3. Ran monthly and quarterly time-series analysis (2011–2014) for seasonality and year-over-year growth.
  4. Built an RFM scoring pipeline in Python that sorts customers into 9 behavioral segments.
  5. Built an interactive Power BI dashboard with custom DAX measures and dynamic filters.
>30% discount: most sub-categories lose money above this level.
Tables & Bookcases: the two sub-categories that consistently lose money.
12% of customers ("Champions") drive over 40% of total revenue.
Problems and how I handled them
ProblemProfit is negative on some orders, so negative values could not simply be dropped as errors.
What I didI checked Sales and Quantity for invalid values but kept the loss-making rows, since they are what the analysis looks for.
ProblemTotal revenue looked fine and hid the sub-categories that lose money.
What I didI added Profit Margin and Discount Range and split results by category, sub-category, region and segment. That showed the losses sit in Tables and Bookcases and above a 30% discount.
ProblemA list of customers is not something a marketing team can act on.
What I didRFM scoring grouped them into 9 segments, and the Power BI dashboard with filters presents those to a non-technical audience.
